blocks.text: Instruction prompting means writing prompts as direct commands, summarize this, translate that, classify the following, rather than as an implied continuation of text, this is the dominant prompting style today, made possible by models specifically trained to follow instructions.

This topic covers what instruction prompting actually is as a distinct technique, the older completion style prompting it largely replaced, why instruction tuned models changed prompting practice, and how this technique interacts with the other techniques covered in this module.
1. What Instruction Prompting Means as a Technique

blocks.alt: Building on role prompting, instruction prompting uses a direct command style

blocks.text: Instruction prompting means phrasing a prompt as an explicit command describing the task, rather than as the start of a passage the model should simply continue, this direct command style is what nearly every modern chat based model interaction actually looks like.
2. The Older Alternative, Completion Style Prompting

blocks.alt: Completion style continues a piece of text, instruction style directly commands a task

blocks.text: Earlier language models were trained purely to predict likely continuations of text, prompting them meant writing the beginning of a passage and letting the model complete it, "The best way to summarize an article is to" rather than directly saying "Summarize this article."

code.content:
# Completion style, older approach
prompt = "The three biggest causes of climate change are"

# Instruction style, modern approach
prompt = "List the three biggest causes of climate change."

blocks.text: 3. Why Instruction Tuned Models Changed Everything

blocks.alt: A base model needs completion style framing, an instruction tuned model accepts direct commands directly

blocks.text: Models specifically fine tuned on large sets of instruction and response pairs, a process covered in the Supervised Fine-Tuning module of the separate Fine-Tuning course, learned to treat a direct command as exactly that, a command to fulfill, rather than text to simply continue, this training is what made instruction prompting the practical default.
4. Direct Commands vs Implied Continuation

blocks.alt: An older completion style prefix is contrasted with a modern direct instruction prompt

blocks.text: The practical difference matters, a completion style prompt relies on the model correctly guessing that you want a specific kind of continuation, an instruction style prompt states the actual goal outright, removing that guesswork entirely, the specificity principles from the earlier Instruction topic in the previous module apply directly here.

blocks.text: 5. Why Instruction Tuning Reduces the Need for Examples

blocks.alt: Training on instruction response pairs lets a model reliably follow direct commands

blocks.text: Because instruction tuned models were specifically trained on many varied instruction and response pairs, they often follow a clear direct command reliably even without any examples included in the prompt, this is part of why zero-shot prompting, covered earlier in this module, works as well as it does on modern instruction tuned models.

blocks.title: This connects directly to the zero-shot topic earlier in this module
blocks.content: Zero-shot prompting relies on the model already understanding how to follow an instruction, that capability specifically comes from instruction tuning, the two topics describe the same underlying mechanism from different angles.

blocks.text: 6. Combining Instruction Prompting With Few-Shot Examples

blocks.alt: Instruction prompting alone is compared against instruction combined with few-shot examples

blocks.text: Instruction prompting and few-shot prompting are not competing techniques, a direct instruction combined with a few representative examples generally performs at least as well as either technique alone, and often better on tasks with a specific output format or edge cases worth demonstrating directly.
7. When You Might Still Encounter Completion Style Prompting

Completion style prompting still shows up in a few specific contexts, working directly with a base model that has not been instruction tuned, or certain code completion and autocomplete style use cases where continuing a partial pattern actually is the intended task.
8. Writing Effective Direct Instructions

blocks.alt: A clear imperative verb leads to reliable task execution

blocks.text: Effective instruction prompts open with a clear, direct imperative verb, summarize, translate, extract, classify, exactly the strong verb guidance covered in the earlier Instruction topic, this consistency across topics reflects that instruction prompting is really that same principle applied as the default interaction style for modern models.
9. Recognizing Whether a Model Is Instruction Tuned

Nearly every widely used commercial model API today, covered in depth in the later LLM APIs Fundamentals module, is instruction tuned by default, a quick way to confirm is testing a direct command style prompt with no examples and checking whether the model responds appropriately to the command rather than simply continuing the text pattern.
Worked Example

A developer working with an older, non instruction tuned base model finds that directly commanding "Summarize this article" produces an odd, unhelpful continuation rather than an actual summary, switching to a completion style prompt, "A concise summary of this article is:", produces the intended result instead.

Switching to a modern instruction tuned model, the original direct command "Summarize this article" now works correctly on its own, demonstrating exactly how instruction tuning changes which prompting style actually works best.
Common Mistakes

items: Writing a completion style prompt for a modern instruction tuned model when a direct command would be simpler and more reliable
Assuming every model handles direct instructions the same way, without checking whether it is actually instruction tuned
Treating instruction prompting and few-shot prompting as mutually exclusive rather than techniques that combine well
Using a weak, indirect phrasing instead of a clear imperative verb to open the instruction

blocks.text: Practice

Take a task you would normally phrase as a direct command, rewrite it in an older completion style instead, run both versions against the same model, and compare which one produces a more directly usable result.
Key Takeaway

Instruction prompting phrases a prompt as a direct command rather than an implied continuation, a style made reliable by models specifically trained on instruction response pairs, and it has become the dominant, default prompting approach for modern instruction tuned models, working well on its own and combining naturally with few-shot examples.
